title: Love the hard way
translation: There are eyes everywhere, and people watching her every move, and you still find a way to get to her. That's the kind of love that leaves you with moments you'll never forget, moments that go deep. If her parents and family say yes and you simply move her into your house, it must be quite embarrassing.

Then there's the woman who is having a hard time and says, like the old poem, "If a stream came to carry me off, I'd go." She means anyone with money will do, even an old priest who is all wrong for her, or some rough man from the east. The go-between makes each side sound wonderful to the other, and a man brings home a woman who has never met him, and whom he has never met. What's the point? What would they even talk about? Two people who can look back together on the hard months and years, and on the thick woods they pushed through to get there, will never run out of things to say.

Anything that outsiders arrange for you is bound to have a lot that's unpleasant. Even if she's a good woman, a man who is lower in rank, ugly and getting old will think, "Why would she waste herself on someone like me?" He'll think less of her for it. Sitting across from her, he'll be ashamed of how he looks. It's no good at all.

Some people will never stand under a hazy moon on a night that smells of plum blossom, or walk home at dawn through the dew by the palace walls, and have that to remember as their own. They're better off without love altogether.
original: しのぶの{浦|うら}の{蜑|あま}のみるめも{所|ところ}{狭|せ}く、くらぶの{山|やま}も{守|も}る{人|ひと}しげからむに、わりなく{通|かよ}はむ{心|こころ}の{色|いろ}こそ、{浅|あさ}からずあはれと{思|おも}ふふしぶしの、{忘|わす}れがたき{事|こと}も{多|おほ}からめ。
{親|おや}はらからゆるして、ひたぶるに{迎|むか}へすゑたらむ、いとまばゆかりぬべし。
{世|よ}にありわぶる{女|をんな}の、{似|に}げなき{老|おい}{法師|ほふし}、{怪|あや}しの{東人|あづまうど}なりとも、{賑|にぎ}ははしきにつきて、「さそふ{水|みづ}あらば。」などいふを、なか{人|びと}いづかたも{心|こころ}にくきさまにいひなして、{知|し}られずしらぬ{人|ひと}を{迎|むか}へもて{来|きた}らむあいなさよ。
{何事|なにごと}をかうち{出|い}づる{言|こと}の{葉|は}にせむ。
{年月|としつき}のつらさをも、{分|わ}けこしは{山|やま}のなどもあひかたらはむこそ、つきせぬ{言|こと}の{葉|は}にてもあらめ。
すべてよその{人|ひと}のとりまかなひたらむ、うたて{心|こころ}づきなき{事|こと}{多|おほ}かるべし。
よき{女|をんな}ならむにつけても、{品|しな}くだり、みにくく、{年|とし}も{長|た}けなむ{男|をとこ}は、「かく{怪|あや}しき{身|み}のために、あたら{身|み}をいたづらになさむやは。」と、{人|ひと}も{心劣|こころおと}りせられ、わが{身|み}はむかひ{居|ゐ}たらむも、{影|かげ}はづかしくおぼえなむ、いとこそあいなからめ。
{梅|うめ}の{花|はな}かうばしき{夜|よ}の{朧月|おぼろづき}にたたずみ、{御垣|みかき}が{原|はら}の{露|つゆ}{分|わ}け{出|い}でむありあけの{空|そら}も、わが{身|み}ざまに{忍|しの}ばるべくもなからむ{人|ひと}は、ただ{色|いろ}{好|この}まざらむにはしかじ。
literal: When the seaweed of the fisherfolk of Shinobu Bay is scarce, and on Mount Kurabu too the guards are many, it is the colour of a heart that goes (to her) regardless that surely has many unforgettable moments that one feels deeply moving.
If parents and siblings permit it and one simply brings her home and settles her there, that must be very embarrassing.

A woman struggling in the world, even (if he is) an unsuitable old priest or a lowly man from the east, attaching herself to wealth, says things like 'if there is water to invite me', and the go-between describes both sides attractively, and (the man) brings home a person who does not know him and whom he does not know: how pointless!
What would they make into words to bring up?
Talking together of the pains of the months and years, and of 'the foothills I came pushing through': that would surely be words without end.
In general, what is arranged by outside people must have many unpleasant, distasteful things.

Even if she is a good woman, a man who is lower in rank, ugly, and advanced in years (thinks), 'Would she waste her precious self for such a lowly person as me?', and comes to think less of her, and he himself, even sitting facing her, would feel ashamed of his appearance: that would surely be very pointless.

A person for whom standing in the hazy moon on a night fragrant with plum blossoms, or the dawn sky as he goes out parting the dew of the palace grounds, could never be something to remember as his own: nothing would be better than simply not loving at all.

notes.quote: しのぶの浦の蜑のみるめも所狭く
notes.text: The opening is built from wordplay that does not survive in English. Shinobu Bay is a place in the north, and しのぶ also means 'to hide, to keep secret'. みるめ is a seaweed, and also 'a chance to see her' ({見|み}る{目|め}), or the eyes of others. {所|ところ}{狭|せ}し: 'cramped, hard to manage'. The 1925 edition explains the pairs. The translation keeps only the meaning: secret love, with little chance to meet.

notes.quote: くらぶの山も守る人しげからむに
notes.text: Mount Kurabu, near the capital, is a poetic place whose name sounds like 'dark' (くら). {守|も}る{人|ひと}: a mountain warden, and also the people who guard a girl. しげし: 'many', and also 'thick with trees' (the 1925 edition's gloss).
{心|こころ}の{色|いろ}: 'the colour of the heart', how deep someone's feeling is. こそ … め: the realis form of む.

notes.quote: いとまばゆかりぬべし
notes.text: まばゆし: 'too bright to look at', and so 'embarrassing, awkward' (the 1925 edition: 'it would make one feel shy'). The modern word まばゆい keeps only the brightness.

From a poem by Ono no Komachi in the Kokinshū, written when Fun'ya no Yasuhide invited her to come with him to the provinces (so the 1925 edition): わびぬれば{身|み}を{浮草|うきくさ}の{根|ね}を{絶|た}えてさそふ{水|みづ}あらばいなむとぞ{思|おも}ふ, 'I am so miserable that, like a floating weed cut from its roots, I would go if a stream came to carry me off.' Here it is just the woman's way of saying that she would take anyone.
{東人|あづまうど}: a man from the eastern provinces, where the warriors of the shogunate came from. To people in the capital they were rough and uncultured, but some were rich. {賑|にぎ}ははし: 'well-off'.
'Someone she is not known to and does not know'. The 1925 edition hears an echo of a Shin Kokinshū poem with the phrase {知|し}らず{知|し}られぬ.

{端山|はやま}: the foothills, thick with trees. The 1925 edition points to a Shin Kokinshū poem: {筑波山|つくばやま}は{山|やま}しげ{山|やま}しげけれど{思|おも}ひ{入|い}るにはさはらざりけり, 'Mount Tsukuba is thick with trees, but nothing stops a heart set on going in.' The lovers can tell each other how hard it was to reach each other.

{心劣|こころおと}り: 'thinking less of someone than before'. 人 here is the woman, as modern commentaries take it: the man cannot help thinking less of her because she accepted him. In せられ, らる is spontaneous: the feeling comes by itself.

notes.quote: 御垣が原の露分け出でむありあけの空
notes.text: {御垣|みかき}が{原|はら}: the grounds inside the palace walls (the 1925 edition's gloss). A lover leaves at first light, through the wet grass. ありあけ: the dawn, when the moon is still in the sky. Both images are the stock of court love poetry.

notes.quote: ただ色好まざらむにはしかじ
notes.text: {色|いろ}{好|この}む: 'to be a lover', in the good sense (compare section 137). には{如|し}かじ: 'nothing is better than'. Section 3 says that a man who doesn't care about love is missing something. Here Kenkō adds the other side: if it will never be like this, don't bother.
